title: The real change India needs
html:
The real change India needs is for people to clean up after themselves and to maintain things. We'll go a long way if we just maintain what's already built. A cult of preservation and maintenance is underrated. Building things is sexy; preserving and maintaining them is not.

title: On brain rot
html:
A thoughtful essay by Mahika Dhar in Public Books on brain rot as political resistance. Please read it.

I want to preface this by saying I could be wrong. This might well be a misreading of her piece. But I came away with a small confusion, and I think it's worth sitting with.

A little mental exercise: replace "brain rot" with "satire" throughout the essay. A lot of the meaning still holds. That makes me wonder if there's a subtle reframing going on. I don't want to make the mistake of suggesting the author doesn't know what she's doing. Right at the outset she points to how fluid the term is, how it can hold a whole lot of meanings. But if you take brain rot in its popular sense, on its own terms, it's vacuous content. Plain nonsense. Not the nonsense of Dylan, or of the poets who used it to poke power in the eye. Just drivel. (And I say this not as one of those hand-wavy critics lamenting the decline of literary culture. That's not my point at all.)

That raises the question of who exactly Mahika means when she says brain rot. It seems to me there are three parties: the people who produce it, the people who consume it, and the people who reuse it. I think the reusers are what she's really getting at, and it's a brilliant point. Even as I write this, the Cockroach Janta Party is back at it, demanding the Chief Election Commissioner resign over the SIR controversy. You can see the same playbook: taking what would otherwise be throwaway brain rot and using it to drive home a political point.

But treating all brain rot as the same doesn't seem quite apt to me. Is all brain rot nonsense? Is all nonsense brain rot? And if there's a sharper point embedded in a piece of brain rot, is it still brain rot? Or has it become satire, sarcasm, absurdist commentary?

Take the ur-example of satire, Swift's A Modest Proposal, where he suggests in a surgical deadpan that the Irish poor sell their children as food for the rich. Run it through the brain rot test. Is it brain rot, or is it satire?

Maybe this is all semantic yogasana on my part, and it obscures Mahika's actual point: that brain rot works as a tool for saying serious things about power. Fair enough. But elevating all brain rot to the same level risks, paradoxically, flattening the very many meanings of the word she points to at the start. You could just as easily swap "brain rot" for "slop" in a lot of cases. What's brain rot to one man is slop to another.

Having said all of this, I think the important point Mahika makes still stands, and it's worth appreciating in full: that brain rot, done well, can be appropriated to speak back to power. It's an underrated point, and not many people have made it. Kudos to Mahika for seeing past the absolutist readings and moving (delving, wink wink) into the nuance.

In a way, it's a new linguistic development, if you think about it. I think we're past the age of manifestos and polemics, that highly intellectualized, Europeanized mode of protest and speaking back. Memes, brain rot, slop have become tools in the linguistic toolkit of a new generation, used to raise grievances, to ask for what's due, to poke power in the eye. In 2026, a good brain rot meme, used well, can do more than a ten-page manifesto.

Is this for the good or the bad? I honestly don't know. And here I must confess I might sound like just another person with a generational gripe, but that's not where I'm coming from. I just don't have a good sense of how this plays out.

title: Gandhi vs Ambedkar
html:
A snippet from this Hindu article with an excerpt from Rama Chandra Guha's Arguments with Gandhi:

Ambedkar saw Gandhi as a timid and hesitant reformer. Orthodox Hindus, on the other hand, saw Gandhi as a dangerous revolutionary attacking the very basis of scripture and tradition. This disjuncture in viewpoints brings to mind some comments of the great black abolitionist Frederick Douglass on his great white contemporary Abraham Lincoln. In a speech of 1876, Douglass remarked that ‘viewed from the genuine abolition ground, Mr. Lincoln seemed tardy, cold, dull, and indifferent; but measuring him by the sentiment of his country, a sentiment he was bound as a statesman to consult, he was swift, zealous, radical, and determined.’

The two greatest opponents of untouchability in the first half of the twentieth century were Gandhi and Ambedkar. Their differing social locations and political affiliations produced sharp disagreements between the two men. In recent decades, as Dalits have grown more self-aware and better organised, they have turned more, much more, to Ambedkar than to Gandhi, to the activist intellectual who was himself a Dalit rather than to the guilt-ridden upper-caste reformer. This elevation of Ambedkar over Gandhi was inevitable, and appropriate. However, the politics of the present have also led to a wholesale repudiation of Gandhi on the part of those who seek to fight against the injustices of caste.

title: Sukumar Sen and India's First Election
html:
I'm reading Ramachandra Guha's magisterial India After Gandhi, and one section stopped me in my tracks: his account of how India conducted its first general election. The scale of it is staggering. Guha walks through the numbers, the infrastructure, the people and the resources it took, and he credits much of it to one man, Sukumar Sen, about whom, as Guha notes, we know very little.

With the country in the middle of important debates over the SIR, the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls, it seems a good moment to step back and see how far we've come. India was one of the first countries to begin its democratic life with universal adult suffrage, rather than expanding the vote bit by bit. Through all the ups and downs since, the right to vote has remained an indispensable part of what it means to be Indian. That history should frame the arguments we're having today.

So I asked Claude to write a short note on Sukumar Sen and the sheer scope of India's first general election. Here it is.

An act of faith

Between October 1951 and February 1952, a country that had been free for barely four years asked roughly 176 million adults to choose their government. Some 85 percent of them could not read or write. Most had never voted for anything, and the world largely doubted it could be done.

It was the largest election humanity had ever attempted, spread over a million square miles of mountains, deserts, jungles and floodplains. The historian Ramachandra Guha has called it an act of faith. The man charged with turning that faith into ballot boxes was a quiet civil servant named Sukumar Sen.

The mathematician in charge

Sen was a Bengali, educated at Presidency College in Calcutta and University College London, where he won a gold medal in mathematics. He joined the Indian Civil Service in 1921 and rose to chief secretary of West Bengal. In March 1950 he was appointed India's first Chief Election Commissioner.

His first and perhaps most important act was to say no. Prime Minister Nehru wanted elections as early as 1951. Sen, whom Guha suspects was thinking like a mathematician, asked him to wait. A census had to finish, election laws had to pass, constituencies had to be drawn, and every adult in the country had to be found and written down. A rushed vote that failed would have discredited democracy itself.

Building the machine

The numbers Guha gathers convey the scale. Nearly 4,500 seats were at stake, about 500 for Parliament and the rest for state assemblies, all elected at once. Some 224,000 polling booths were set up and about two million steel ballot boxes were made. More than 56,000 presiding officers ran the booths, backed by some 280,000 support staff and roughly as many police as there were booths.

The rolls were the first hurdle. Thousands of clerks were hired to compile them by hand. In parts of northern India, women would not give their own names, only "wife of" or "mother of" some man. Sen called this a senseless relic and ordered officials to record real names. About 2.8 million women who could not be properly identified were struck off, a painful price he accepted to keep the rolls honest.

He also had to design a vote for people who could not read. Each candidate got a pictorial symbol, such as a pair of bullocks, a hut or a lamp. Instead of marking a ballot, voters dropped a paper into the box carrying their candidate's symbol. Mock polls were staged in 1951 to test the system, films and radio talks explained it, and phials of ink, nearly 390,000 by Guha's count, were used to mark voters' fingers against fraud.

The vote

Polling was staggered over about four months so that officials, boxes and police could move across the country. Snowbound hill districts voted first, in late October 1951, before winter closed the passes. A schoolteacher from Kalpa in Himachal Pradesh, Shyam Saran Negi, is remembered as the first person to cast a vote in independent India; he kept voting into his hundreds.

The rest of the country followed through early 1952. Turnout was roughly 45 percent, remarkable for a first-time electorate. The Congress Party won a large majority, and Nehru became India's first democratically elected prime minister. Just as important, the losers accepted the result.

A forgotten founder

The success made Sen briefly famous abroad. Sudan invited him to oversee its first election in 1953, and India gave him the Padma Bhushan in 1954. He ran the second general election in 1957 too, using ballot boxes salvaged from the first, and left office in 1958. He died in 1963.

Yet Guha laments how little we know about him. He left no memoir, and his name rarely appears beside Nehru, Patel or Ambedkar. That may be the truest measure of what he achieved. Sen built a process so trusted that Indians came to take it for granted, and a democracy that the world expected to fail has held elections ever since.

Further reading

  • Ramachandra Guha, India After Gandhi (2007), chapter "The Biggest Gamble in History" — the best-known account. An extract is online at The Caravan.
  • Ornit Shani, How India Became Democratic (2017) — how the electoral rolls were built from 1947 onward, even before Sen took charge.
  • Election Commission of India, Report on the First General Elections in India 1951-52 — Sen's own two-volume official account.
  • Election Commission of India, Leap of Faith — an illustrated history dedicated to Sen.
  • Chambers Book of Indian Election Facts (Hachette India) — figures and anecdotes; see the Mainstream review.

Note: sources differ on the ink. Guha records ink used in 1951-52, while others date the modern indelible ink to the 1962 election.

title: A tale of two Chinas
html:
Nice note from BlackRock:

Outside China, the key question is whether companies use Chinese technology or compete against it. Cheaper Chinese industrial robots and machinery can boost productivity and ease labor shortages for their customers. For rival producers, the economics are less appealing. European machinery makers illustrate the squeeze. China has moved from a major buyer of advanced machinery to a formidable competitor at home and abroad. In 2025, it overtook Germany as the world’s largest machine-tool exporter for the first time.

iAI creates a similar divide. Cheaper Chinese models could accelerate AI adoption while commoditizing the model market. That could shift value toward the physical infrastructure needed to support greater AI use - computing power, data centers and electricity - reinforcing the scarcity investment theme from our Midyear Global Outlook. Physical AI could amplify demand for power electronics and batteries while broadening demand for components like motors and actuators – areas where China already has a manufacturing and supply-chain advantage. But technology sovereignty cuts both ways: export controls and efforts to reduce reliance on Chinese technology could limit market access. That makes geopolitics a key risk to where the opportunity ultimately lies.

Inside China, industrial policy has helped build scale and competitiveness, but growth alone does not guarantee shareholder returns. Long-standing challenges – including weak domestic consumption, a soft property market and an aging population – remain, while intense competition can squeeze margins even in industries where China has gained global market shares. The divergence is stark: profits at Chinese electronic-device makers rose 110% year over year in the first seven months of 2026, supported by global AI demand, while auto profits fell 20.4%, according to data from the National Bureau of Statistics of China. Likewise, AI hardware suppliers have expanded margins, while solar manufacturers have seen theirs collapse. Markets echo that divide: the MSCI China index has lost 11% in U.S. dollar terms this year through Sept. 21, while the MSCI China Information Technology index has gained 7%.

title: Indian government sucks at industrial policy
html:
Raghuram Rajan on industrial policy:

I’d say that I am not against the government’s actions; I am very much for the government’s actions on dealing with the fundamentals. So let’s focus on public goods such as education and healthcare, let’s focus on building good roads, let’s focus on creating a good business environment, let’s focus on utilities, let’s focus on water, electricity, logistics. These are areas where you have a much better chance of success improving things rather than [picking winners and sectors].

Whenever our government showers a sector with love, it has not ended particularly well except for the areas I just mentioned. Kudos to the current government for building out Indian infrastructure. That’s great. But I think if you test them on manufacturing, have they really created more manufacturing jobs? The line is flat [on the chart]. Look at the line. I’d say that just the evidence suggests that we have not been great. Maybe some other countries have seen success.

title: Sales of weight loss drugs in India
html:
The weight loss revolution in India seems to be doing ok?

And right on cue, the fakes have arrived on the scene:

Spurious drugs are a recurring problem in India, said Mahesh Zagade, a former commissioner of the Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration. He said that while the country’s laws are robust, implementation and enforcement have been lacking. Short-staffed regulators, the possibility of corruption, and easy access to raw materials have contributed to the problem, in his view. “This is a failure of the official machinery,” he said, adding that until action is taken to fix the broader system, “this situation is just not going to improve.”

title: Begum Aizaz Rasul
html:
What a legend. Came across the name for the first time in India after Gandhi:

With the enactment of the Government of India Act 1935, the couple joined the Muslim League and entered electoral politics. In the 1937 elections, she was one of the few women who successfully contested from a non-reserved seat and was elected to the U.P legislative assembly. Begum Aijaz Rasul remained a member until 1952. She held the office of the Deputy President of the council from 1937 to 1940 and acted as the Leader of Opposition in the council from 1950 to 1952–54. She was the first woman in India and the first Muslim woman in the world to reach this position. Despite her family background, she was known for her strong support for zamindari abolition. She also strongly opposed the demand for separate electorates based on religion.

In 1946, she was elected to the Constituent Assembly of India and was one of 28 Muslim League members who finally joined. She was the only Muslim woman in the Assembly. In 1950, the Muslim League in India dissolved and Begum Aijaz Rasul joined the Congress. She was elected to the Rajya Sabha in 1952-54 and was a member of the Uttar Pradesh Legislative Assembly from 1969 to 1989.

Between 1969 and 1971, she was the Minister for Social Welfare and Minorities. In 2000, she was awarded a Padma Bhushan for her contribution to social work.[2]
